The invention relates to a machine learning system (10). It is described as providing (110) input data to a processing unit. The processing unit processes (120) the input data to generate processing path input data. A processing unit implementation (130) includes a first processing path of a feedforward neural network to process the processing path input data to generate first intermediate data. The processing unit implements (140) a second processing path comprising a feedforward neural network to process the processing path input data to generate second intermediate data, wherein the second processing path is random. The processing unit implements (150) a value output path including a feedforward neural network to process the first intermediate data and the second intermediate data to generate value output data. The processing unit implements (160) a policy output path including a feedforward neural network to process the first intermediate data and the second intermediate data to generate policy output data. The output unit outputs (170) the value output data and the policy output data.

Machine learning systemTechnical Field

The invention relates to a machine learning system and a method for implementing the machine learning system.

Background

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine learning framework developed to empirically learn a near-optimal control strategy for a physical device or software system. In the RL, a controller (also called agent) needs to explore the space of available states and actions to be controlled and receive a so-called reward signal indicating the success of the strategy being followed. Importantly, whether or not each individual action taken is optimal, the rewards are typically not immediately signaled, but may be given with delay or in a random fashion only after a series of actions. Thus, there is a need to address the difficult confidence allocation problem that decides which of the previously taken actions should be noted as being used for rewarding (rewards may also be negative if false actions are taken). The main objectives of the RL algorithm are:

seeking the best possible strategy for the control problem, namely, a strategy for realizing the maximum overall rewards; and

Learning as fast as possible an optimal strategy by means of intelligent exploration strategies, namely trying actions with unknown outcome without risking a large negative reward (which may for example correspond to damage to the controlled physical system), and maximizing the information obtained about the system to be controlled.

While general reinforcement learning algorithms have been known for decades, they have only become possible in recent years to cope with very difficult scenarios characterized by very large or even continuous (and thus infinite) states and motion spaces, as well as complex dynamics of the system to be controlled. Early RL algorithms were based on the following assumptions: each state-action pair can be explored at will often and a cost function can be learned that estimates a viable expected prize from each possible state or for a state-action pair. However, this concept is only useful for discrete spaces and becomes infeasible for the very large states and action spaces of interest herein. One major breakthrough is the combination of RL and Deep learning, known as Deep RL. This concept uses Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to learn meaningful abstractions of high-dimensional state signals, and/or uses DNNs to approximate policies and cost functions.

Mnih et al, "Asynchronous methods for deep reinforcement learning (asynchronous method for deep reinforcement learning)" (JMLR:W & CP, volume 48) at 33 rd machine learning International conference (33 rd International Conference on MACHINE LEARNING, new York, NY, USA, 2016) held in 2016 N.Y. in N.Y. developed an asynchronous dominant motion-assessment algorithm (A3C). A3C is a fast, robust, lightweight, model-free depth RL algorithm that achieves in-field representative results on many complex game tasks such as yadari 2600 (Atari 2600), viz-doom, and mini-interstellar dispute (mini-STARCRAFT). In A3C, multiple agents are generated to interact with the environment simultaneously with different random seeds and optimize a shared model that approximates functions of both strategy and value by asynchronous gradient descent. The A3C algorithm is schematically shown in fig. 1. The A3C algorithm consists of: a feed-forward Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract features from a high-dimensional input signal (e.g., raw visual input); cycling the LSTM (long term memory) neural network to merge the time dependencies from previous steps; a value network to approximate value; and a policy network to approximate policies. The inputs are processed by the CNN and fed into the torus network (LSTM). The output of the LSTM is then mapped to a cost function and policy using two different networks. In A3C, all networks are deterministic. On the left side of fig. 1, the network used during training is shown, and on the right side, the network used during testing is shown. The network is the same for A3C, except that two different types of action selections are performed for the policy network (sample against highest likelihood action). During training, A3C samples its actions from the approximate policy distribution; during testing, A3C takes the action with the highest likelihood in the discrete case. The ownership weights in A3C-LSTM are always determined and the activation is also always determined. During training, actions are sampled from the policy distribution. During testing/evaluation, actions are selected as the strategy with the highest likelihood.

"Noise Networks for Exploration (noise network for exploration)" by Fortunato et al published as a conference paper on ICLR 2018 developed a noisy network (NoisyNet), a deep reinforcement learning agent with parametric noise added to its weights. The "PARAMETER SPACE Noise for Exploration (parameter spatial noise for exploration)" of Plappert et al published as conference paper on ICLR 2018 combines parameter spatial noise with existing algorithms. In the paper of Fortunato et al, a Deep Q Network (DQN), a variant of Q-learning algorithm and A3C deep learning without LSTM framework, was used; the weights obey a gaussian distribution with a learned mean and variance. DQN and policy gradient framework were used in Plappert et al; the weights also obey gaussian distribution but have an adaptive variance based on the distance between the current strategy and the perturbation strategy. During the test, the weights were fixed as the average of the gaussian distribution. Such development is referred to as noisy network A3C (NoisyNet A C), at a high level this series of models generally inject noise into the model parameters during training to motivate exploration. The models are shown in combination in fig. 2, however, although the architecture discussed above is similar to A3C, during training the output network (value network and policy network) is random.

However, in such machine learning systems, randomness in the dynamics of the controlled system and also lack of training data may lead to imperfect approximations and thus sub-optimal decisions.

Disclosure of Invention

It would therefore be advantageous to have an improved machine learning system and method of implementing a machine learning system.

The object of the invention is solved by the subject matter of the independent claims, wherein further embodiments are incorporated in the dependent claims. It should be noted that the following described aspects of the invention also apply to the machine learning system and the method of implementing the machine learning system, as well as to the computer program element and the computer readable medium.

In a first aspect, there is provided a machine learning system comprising:

An input unit;

a processing unit; and

And an output unit.

The input unit is configured to provide input data to the processing unit. The processing unit is configured to process the input data to generate processing path input data. The processing unit is configured to implement a first processing path including a feedforward neural network to process processing path input data to generate first intermediate data. The processing unit is configured to implement a second processing path comprising a feedforward neural network to process the processing path input data to generate second intermediate data, wherein the second processing path is random. The processing unit is configured to implement a value output path including a feedforward neural network to process the first intermediate data and the second intermediate data to generate value output data. The processing unit is configured to implement a policy output path including a feedforward neural network to process the first intermediate data and the second intermediate data to generate policy output data. The output unit is configured to output the value output data and to output the policy output data.

In other words, random implicit elements are explicitly introduced after processing the high-dimensional input signal with the neural network in order to achieve efficient exploration in an uncertain environment.

In this way, reinforcement Learning (RL) within a machine learning framework is used to empirically learn a near optimal control strategy for a physical device or software system.

The system is able to cope with uncertainties arising from the dynamic randomness of the controlled system and from the lack of any training data that may otherwise lead to imperfect approximations and sub-optimal decisions.

Thus, the problem of depth RL in environments that exhibit significant environmental uncertainty is solved.

Faster convergence is provided because fewer training data can be utilized and the strategy can be learned in a shorter time, which reduces the cost for learning the control strategy. If the controlled system comprises physical equipment, wear on the equipment is also reduced and there is a lower risk of damaging the equipment during training.

With the exploration of improvements due to the random units that lead to learning a better strategy, a better learning strategy is achieved. This means that the device being controlled performs better, e.g. faster, safer, less risky, more cost-effective, which may depend on how the reward function is defined.

Enabling better exploration. Because of the randomness of the cells, the controller can explore the state and action space more efficiently and can randomly choose actions in the presence of uncertainty. This provides better coverage for all relevant state-action combinations during training.

Advantageously, the benefits provided by any of the above aspects apply equally to all other aspects and vice versa.

The above aspects and examples will become apparent from and will be elucidated with reference to the embodiments described hereinafter.

The machine learning system 10 of fig. 3 and the method of fig. 4 implementing the machine learning system 100 are now described in further detail with reference to fig. 5.

As discussed above with reference to fig. 3-4, the machine learning system developed herein addresses the problem of reinforcement learning to achieve near optimal control strategies for some physical or virtual systems in the shortest possible time. RL is particularly useful in scenarios where analytical methods from control theory cannot be applied, for example because the system to be controlled is too complex, or there are many uncertain factors (e.g. reactions of other agents in the environment). In particular, the problem of learning strategies under various forms of uncertainty is solved.

Uncertainty is a core topic in decision making not only for machines but also for humans. Similar to human decision making, it is also necessary for general machine learning algorithms to take into account uncertainties, for example, regarding perceived states, or regarding the outcome of selected actions. Furthermore, training of machine learning models often suffers from additional forms of uncertainty, referred to as model uncertainty, due to lack of data that results in imperfect parameter estimation or even imperfect model architecture selection.

Not only does the reinforcement learning problem inherit all of the uncertainties that are common in a general machine learning setup, but it is further challenged by a new layer of uncertainty: the dynamics of its environment, such as uncertainty in the rewards.

The machine learning system developed herein and shown in fig. 5 alleviates these problems by: random implicit elements are explicitly introduced after processing the high-dimensional input signal with the neural network in order to achieve efficient exploration in an uncertain environment.

In contrast to the baseline A3C representative of the field described with reference to fig. 1, the machine learning system and associated method as shown in fig. 5 involves random activation during training and testing, while A3C has a certain activation and a certain policy during testing time. By adding a random component, the system and method of fig. 5 allows for more efficient exploration based on maximum flexibility (softmax) sampling for actions, which results in faster convergence and better performance of the final learned strategy. This has been experimentally confirmed in various baseline problems. In addition, the system and method of FIG. 5 also provides a random strategy when the correct answer is ambiguous due to dynamic uncertainty

The system and method of fig. 5 applies randomness in the activation, as compared to the parametric spatial noise described with reference to fig. 2. The benefit of doing so is primarily due to the long sequence of LSTM for each training iteration. Adding a different randomness at each step causes a more complex change in policy than a fixed randomness in the parameters for the entire LSTM sequence. Thus, a better exploration is achieved and secondly more flexibility in how to build random cells depending on the RL problem at hand is obtained. As a result, the system and method of fig. 5 achieves a greatly improved final strategy compared to noisy networks.

Thus, referring to FIG. 5, a reinforcement learning RL system and method, referred to herein as random feedforward A3C (SFA 3C), has been developed. As shown, the architecture shares some similarities with A3C, but processes the output of LSTM in two different paths, one deterministic (active 1) and the second random (active 2). The output network (value network and policy network) receives as input the result of the combination of the determined path and the random path, but as discussed below, the determined path can also be random.

Continuing from fig. 5, the intrinsic mechanism is a collection of different neural networks designed in a way to map an input image into two output signals, one being a cost function and the second being a policy. The framework consists of the following components:

convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that receives an input image and creates abstract feature vectors through nonlinear mapping and pooling operations of one or more layers.

A recurrent neural network of the LSTM type that receives the output of the CNN and maps it to another eigenvector ht that depends on the output of the CNN and the previous activation ht-1 of LSTM (where t is a discrete time index).

Two parallel paths that convert the output ht of LSTM into two abstract feature vectors. It is important and in particular one of the paths is random (active 2) in SFA3C (but not in A3C) and the second path is usually deterministic (active 1) but may also be random in alternative embodiments. These can be described by a fully connected neural network with zero or more hidden layers or other types of feed forward networks (e.g., CNNs).

Two output networks that convert the output of the concatenation of both the determined path and the random path into a cost function and a policy. This can be implemented by a fully connected neural network with zero or more hidden layers or other types of feed forward networks.

Random path

An important part of SFA3C is the random path following LSTM layers, compared to other architectures such as A3C. The SFA3C is designed in the following way: immediately following the output ht from the LSTM, the next hidden layer is divided into a deterministic path (active 1) and a random path (active 2). The determined path kt=fdet (ht) is parameterized with the full connectivity layer. Random implicit cells obey a factored gaussian distribution. There are two variations in the mean value of the inferred random cells. The simplest version is state independent: i.e. the global average is learned irrespective of the current state. While this version of SFA3C is as simple as it is, it can actually improve performance on the environment with simple exploration settings. However, as expected, state independent noise may become a problem once a more complex exploration is required. Thus, a state-dependent variant is introduced, in which the mean value is deduced from the calculation of the function μt=fmean (ht) of the output of LSTM, and the parameterization is performed with fully connected layers, similar to the determined cells. In both cases, the variance σt is fixed to a certain value that is selected as the hyper-parameter. A variant is possible in which the variance can also be calculated as a function of the output of LSTM, i.e. σt=fvar (ht).

Forwarding new images through a neural network implementing SFA3C is similar to A3C-LSTM (Mnih et al), but with the following differences: for random units, samples are created from a gaussian distribution according to zt-N (μt, σt) and concatenated with kt as input for the policy and value networks. Training the network via back propagation through random cells is accomplished by performing a re-parameterization to reduce the variance of the gradient.

Finally, other variations of the random unit SFA3C can be derived based on this basic idea, including replacing the determined part and constructing a completely random SFA3C and adding an additional a priori to regularize the parameters of the distribution for the random unit.

Alternate implementation

The following modifications are possible in principle:

Instead of CNN, an additional feed-forward network with zero or more hidden layers can be used to extract abstract features from the image.

Instead of LSTM networks, any type of round robin network can be used, such as a gated round robin unit (GRU) or a pool network.

Different types of feed forward networks can be used to convert the output of the LSTM layer into an output for a cost function or policy. These networks can also be cycled in principle.

Random paths can use arbitrary random distributions.

The random number generator can be a physical generator using, for example, thermal noise or a pseudo-random number generator in software.

As described with respect to fig. 3-5, the new machine learning system and method of implementing the machine learning system find use as follows:

A controller for engines, valves, electrical circuits, heating systems that are too complex to be resolved using analytical methods. The system and method can lead to faster and more economical learning of the final control strategy, as well as better final strategies.

Control of a robotic arm, aerial target, or humanoid robot, for example, for home robots or for use in manufacturing. Robots can use the system and method to expedite learning of manipulation or grasping strategies in unknown and uncertain environments. A controller for a self-driving vehicle that is capable of learning complex maneuvers based on one or more high-dimensional sensor inputs (e.g., cameras, lidar, radar, or ultrasound). Physical or virtual agents that perform online learning, either by changing their control strategies to improve their functionality or to adapt to changes in their environment.
